one_line_idea: Average-case membership metrics hide a vulnerable tail whose size is set by the duplication spectrum: TPR at very low FPR is high for a predictable subset even when aggregate AUC looks safe.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-encoder membership studies often report modest average AUC and conclude low risk, while the security-relevant statistic (true-positive rate at very low false-positive rate) is known from classifier work to behave differently from averages.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Membership risk in web-trained encoders is concentrated: a small subset of images (high-duplication, high-atypicality) is confidently identifiable at 0.1% FPR even when population AUC is near 0.6, and the vulnerable-subset size is predictable from the corpus duplication and density spectra alone.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On encoder trainings with realistic duplication spectra, at least 1% of training images will be detectable at TPR 20x the FPR at 0.1% FPR, and the size of this subset will be predicted within 2x by a duplication-density model fitted on a different corpus; the idea is falsified if the low-FPR regime shows TPR under 5x FPR for all subsets (no vulnerable tail) or subset-size predictions err by over 5x.
why_important: Privacy conclusions drawn from average AUC are the norm in vision; demonstrating a predictable vulnerable tail would invalidate safe-on-average claims and supply the corrected reporting statistic.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Low-FPR evaluation is established as the right metric for classifiers (membership inference from first principles); its application to vision encoders with a data-level predictor of tail size appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train encoders on corpora with measured duplication spectra, run per-example strong attacks, compute full TPR-FPR curves, and test tail-size predictions from the data-level model.
main_risk: Estimating TPR at 0.1% FPR needs large member and non-member pools; underpowered evaluation would produce noisy tail estimates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Modest average membership AUC on encoders is read as encoders are hard to attack, and reporting practice follows averages.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vision-specific augmentation may genuinely protect even duplicated atypical images, emptying the vulnerable tail that classifier intuitions predict.

one_line_idea: Membership signals transfer across models trained on overlapping crawls: an attack fitted on a small open encoder identifies members of a large closed encoder's corpus, because web-crawl overlap makes membership a property of the image, not the model.

main_risk: Transfer may be driven almost entirely by duplication-heavy head content, making the auditable stratum small and legally less interesting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Membership inference is assumed to require attack access fitted to the specific target model and its data distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Idiosyncratic training choices (augmentation, mixture weights) may decorrelate per-image signals across models enough to destroy transfer.

one_line_idea: Distilled students inherit their teacher's membership secrets: distillation on disjoint transfer data still moves enough per-example signal that the teacher's training members are detectable from the student alone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distillation is widely believed to launder privacy: since the student never sees the teacher's training data, releasing only the student is treated as a privacy barrier.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Teacher outputs on transfer data encode member-specific idiosyncrasies (sharper predictions near memorized content), and students fit these idiosyncrasies, so membership of teacher-training images remains detectable from student outputs at levels well above chance even with disjoint transfer sets.

why_important: Distillation-as-privacy-laundering is an operating assumption in industrial model release; quantifying leakage through the distillation channel either breaks or certifies a widely used practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distillation privacy has been studied for classifiers in specific settings; the encoder-scale question with disjoint transfer data and quantified leakage retention appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain a teacher with an injected panel, distill students on disjoint data at 2 capacities, and attack students for panel membership with feature- and output-based attacks.
main_risk: Leakage magnitude likely depends on transfer-set similarity to the teacher corpus; a similarity sweep is needed for the claim to be actionable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Never-saw-the-data is treated as sufficient for privacy, making distilled releases exempt from pretraining-data scrutiny.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Student compression may act as an information bottleneck that preferentially discards member-specific idiosyncrasies, genuinely laundering membership.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 1 teacher pretrain, 2 distillations, plus attacks on public data, one A100: about 5 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Bigger is not leakier at web scale: at fixed unique data, membership risk grows with model size, but along the realistic joint-scaling path (data grows with model) per-image risk falls, inverting the intuitive scale-risk narrative.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Public discussion assumes larger foundation models are automatically worse for privacy, but model releases scale data alongside parameters, and the two effects on per-image exposure act in opposite directions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image membership signal increases with capacity at fixed data but decreases with data at fixed capacity (exposure dilution), and along compute-optimal joint scaling the dilution effect dominates, so newer larger releases are less attackable per ordinary image while remaining attackable on the duplicated tail.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a grid crossing model size with data size, membership AUC will rise with capacity at fixed data (at least +0.05 per 4x capacity) and fall along the joint-scaling diagonal (at least -0.04 per diagonal step) for typical images, while high-duplication images stay flat within 0.03; the idea is falsified if AUC rises along the diagonal for typical images, confirming the bigger-is-leakier narrative.
why_important: The result determines whether scale is a privacy problem or (with data discipline) a privacy mitigation, directly informing policy debates that currently assume the former.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Capacity and data effects on membership risk are known separately; the joint-scaling-path analysis with duplication stratification appears unmeasured for vision encoders.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 3x3 model-size by data-size grid, attack each with a fixed strong attack, stratify results by duplication, and read effects along axes and the diagonal.
main_risk: The diagonal conclusion depends on the assumed joint-scaling policy; results must be reported for at least two plausible scaling paths.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Larger models are assumed monotonically riskier for training-data privacy regardless of accompanying data growth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bigger models may memorize the tail so much more efficiently that even ordinary-image risk rises along realistic scaling paths.

one_line_idea: Collection-level membership auditing: aggregating weak per-image signals across a photographer's or institution's entire collection yields high-confidence dataset-inclusion tests even when every individual image is undetectable.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Consent and copyright disputes concern collections (a portfolio, a hospital archive, a stock library), but membership tools test single images, where signals on well-generalized encoders are usually too weak for confident claims.

one_line_idea: More data can hurt minorities of the distribution: at fixed mixture, growing total data amplifies majority-domain dominance and can reduce absolute accuracy on minority domains, a non-monotonicity fixable by share re-weighting, not by more data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Data growth under a fixed collection mixture is universally assumed at-worst-neutral for every subpopulation, and minority-domain regressions between model releases are treated as accidents rather than a predictable scaling phenomenon.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With fixed mixture weights, scaling total data grows the majority-domain gradient signal proportionally while minority-domain representations face increasing competitive pressure for shared capacity, so beyond a threshold, minority-domain accuracy declines in absolute terms even as aggregate accuracy improves, and share re-weighting at the same total data eliminates the decline.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In fixed-mixture scaling runs spanning 16x total data with a 2% minority domain, minority-domain accuracy will peak and then decline by at least 2 points by the largest scale while aggregate accuracy rises, and a re-weighted arm at the largest scale will recover the minority peak within 1 point; the idea is falsified if minority accuracy is monotone non-decreasing in total data (within 0.5 points) at fixed mixture.
why_important: It would overturn the universal more-data-is-safe assumption at the subpopulation level, explain cross-release regressions that currently look like bugs, and hand corpus owners a costless fix (re-weighting) with measured effect.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Capacity competition and majority dominance are known qualitatively in multi-task settings; the absolute-decline-with-total-data prediction at fixed mixture for vision pretraining appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain across nested total-data sizes at fixed mixture including a tagged 2% minority domain, evaluate minority-domain probes per size, and run a re-weighted control at the largest size.
main_risk: The effect size likely depends on model capacity relative to data; a capacity-matched second ladder is needed to show the decline is not an artifact of one undersized model.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scaling data at fixed composition is believed to help every subpopulation, or at worst leave minorities flat.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-feature transfer from majority growth may keep lifting minority domains indefinitely, making the predicted decline unobservable at feasible scales.
fastest_falsification_experiment: 5-6 small pretrains over nested sizes plus a re-weighted arm, one A100: about 5 GPU-days on public data.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: total data size at fixed mixture versus re-weighted control (data-level)
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: minority-domain accuracy trajectories versus aggregate
